1.title: Task Decomposition, Sessions, Resume and Fork
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Task Decomposition, Sessions, Resume and Fork. This module covers task statements one point six and one point seven: task decomposition, sessions, resume and fork. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Prompt chaining (fixed sequential steps) versus dynamic, adaptive decomposition. Splitting a large review into per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass. Decomposing an open-ended task by mapping first, then planning. Named session resumption, fork session, and when to start fresh with a summary instead of resuming.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply Reviews a Big Change
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply Reviews a Big Change. A pull request changes twelve files of the checkout module. A separate request asks the agent to "add tests to the legacy order system", a codebase nobody fully understands. The two jobs need different ways of breaking work down.

1.title: Choosing a Decomposition Strategy
1.text: Choosing a Decomposition Strategy. Idea. Prompt chaining (fixed pipeline): Break the job into known sequential steps; each step's output feeds the next. Dynamic adaptive decomposition: Let what you discover decide the next subtasks. Use when. Prompt chaining (fixed pipeline): The aspects are predictable: multi-aspect reviews, standard report building. Dynamic adaptive decomposition: The task is open-ended: unfamiliar code, investigations. Example. Prompt chaining (fixed pipeline): Analyze each file, then run a cross-file integration pass. Dynamic adaptive decomposition: Map the structure, find high-impact areas, write a prioritized plan, adapt as dependencies appear.

1.title: Choosing a Decomposition Strategy, continued
1.text: Choosing a Decomposition Strategy, continued. The figure shows this: Prompt chaining suits predictable multi-step work; dynamic decomposition suits open-ended tasks where each finding changes the plan. Exam tip: "Predictable aspects" to prompt chaining. "Unfamiliar, open-ended" to dynamic decomposition.

1.title: Reviewing many files: local passes plus an integration pass
1.text: Reviewing many files: local passes plus an integration pass. One pass over twelve files gives uneven depth (thorough for some files, shallow for others), missed bugs and contradictory feedback (a pattern flagged in one file and approved in another). The cause is attention dilution. Fix: one focused pass per file for local issues, then a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow and interfaces. A bigger context window, or asking developers to shrink the pull request, does not fix the quality of attention; and requiring two of three runs to agree would hide real bugs found only once.

1.title: Open-ended tasks ("add tests to the legacy system")
1.text: Open-ended tasks ("add tests to the legacy system"). Map the structure (modules, entry points). Identify high-impact areas (critical or untested code). Create a prioritized plan. Work through it and adapt as new dependencies are discovered. Exam tip: A big pull request reviewed unevenly means attention dilution: per-file passes plus an integration pass, not a bigger context window.

1.title: Session State, Resumption and Forking
1.text: Session State, Resumption and Forking. A session is the stored conversation (prompts, tool calls, results). You can come back to it later. Continue a specific named investigation across work sessions. Use: Named session resumption. Command or option: claude dash dash resume less than session-name greater than (give names with claude dash n "name" or slash rename). Try two approaches from the same analyzed baseline. Use: fork session. Command or option: claude dash dash resume less than id greater than dash dash fork session (S D K: resume plus fork Session). Prior context is mostly still valid. Use: Resume. Command or option: Add a note about what changed. Prior tool results are stale (files changed). Use: Start a new session with an injected structured summary. Command or option: Summary of findings, not raw old output.

1.title: Session State, Resumption and Forking, continued
1.text: Session State, Resumption and Forking, continued. The figure shows this: Resume when the prior context is mostly valid, tell the agent what changed, and start fresh with a structured summary when the old tool results are stale. Fork creates independent branches from a shared baseline, for example comparing two testing strategies or two refactorings. Each branch keeps its own history; the original is unchanged. When you resume after code changes, tell the agent which files changed so it re-analyzes just those, rather than trusting stale reads or re-exploring everything.

1.title: Session State, Resumption and Forking, continued
1.text: Session State, Resumption and Forking, continued. Why a fresh session with a summary can beat a resume: old tool results may no longer match the files, and the model may keep acting on them.

1.title: Session State, Resumption and Forking, continued
1.text: Session State, Resumption and Forking, continued. In current Claude Code, dash dash resume accepts a session I D or name, dash dash fork session creates a new session I D when resuming, and the Agent S D K (software development kit) offers resume and fork session or fork Session options. A fork branches the conversation, not the files: edits made in a fork are real. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Stale results after code changes: tell the resumed session which files changed, or start fresh with a summary. Never trust old tool output.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Prompt chaining: Fixed sequential steps for predictable multi-aspect work. Dynamic decomposition: Plan adapts to discoveries; for open-ended tasks (map to prioritize to adapt). Large review: Per-file local passes plus integration pass (cures attention dilution). Resume: dash dash resume less than name greater than; tell the agent which files changed. Fork: fork session or dash dash fork session: independent branches from one baseline (conversation only). Fresh start: When tool results are stale: new session plus structured summary.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A pull request changes twelve files, and a single-pass review gives deep feedback on some files, shallow comments on others, and contradicts itself across files. How should the review be restructured? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The problem is attention dilution. Per-file passes plus an integration pass give consistent depth and still catch cross-file issues.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. For which task is dynamic adaptive decomposition the best fit? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Open-ended work needs a plan that adapts to what is discovered. The others are predictable.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A team wants a repeatable analysis for every pull request: security, style, tests, then a summary. The aspects never change. Which strategy fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Predictable multi-aspect work, with aspects that never change, suits a fixed chain of steps.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An engineer analyzed a payment module yesterday in a named session. Overnight, two files changed. What is the best way to continue? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The prior context is mostly valid; informing the agent of the changed files gives targeted re-analysis.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. After a week, a session's saved tool results come from a repository that has been heavily refactored. What is the most reliable approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Stale tool results are risky; a fresh session seeded with a summary is more reliable than resuming.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. An engineer wants to compare a refactor to repository classes with a refactor to service classes, both starting from the same codebase analysis. Which mechanism fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Forking branches from a shared analysis so each approach develops separately.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. What does a fork of a session branch? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Forking copies the conversation, not the file system; file edits in a fork are real.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Select two. Which two tasks are best served by dynamic adaptive decomposition? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Open-ended work where each finding changes the next step needs an adaptive plan. Templates, linting and mechanical edits follow predictable steps.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: B. Question two: C. Question three: D. Question four: A. Question five: B. Question six: A. Question seven: B. Question eight: B and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
